release-ref.question: Our release job reviewed Git commit A as the current release tip before building candidate B. Another maintainer then moved the release ref to C. The job must never overwrite a tip it hasn't reviewed. Its git update-ref refs/heads/release B A failed. A teammate suggests reading C and automatically retrying the same candidate with C as the expected old value. Should we accept that fallback? What should the job do now?
release-ref.answer:
Short answer: reject the fallback. The failed CAS is the job telling you the tip moved; "read C and retry with C as the old value" turns that safety signal into a blind overwrite.

Why, from the git reference (git-update-ref, https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref):

- The three-argument form is a compare-and-swap. The doc says it "updates the ... head to <new-oid> only if its current value is <old-oid>", and "If all <ref>s can be locked with matching <old-oid>s ... all modifications are performed. Otherwise, no modifications are performed."
- So `git update-ref refs/heads/release B A` failed *because* the tip was no longer A (it's C), and git changed nothing. The ref is still C. That failure is not a transient error to retry blindly; it is exactly the guard doing its job.

Why the teammate's retry is wrong:

- `update-ref release B C` sets the expected-old to whatever the ref currently holds. That CAS is guaranteed to match — it re-reads the value and asserts equality with itself. It no longer detects "the tip moved"; it just performs a plain overwrite.
- It overwrites C — a tip the job has *not* reviewed — with B — a candidate built and validated against A. That is precisely what "never overwrite a tip it hasn't reviewed" forbids.
- The CAS only guards the window between read and write. It does *not* establish that the job reviewed the new tip, and it does *not* check ancestry (a CAS moves the ref forward, backward, or sideways alike). Adopting C as the expected value papers over all three. The bug is the review step, not a race.

What the job should do now:

1. Stop this publish. Don't write B; the ref is still C.
2. Re-read the current tip. It is C.
3. Re-run the review against C. "Read C" is not "review C." The job must re-evaluate the release as it now stands at C. Concretely this usually means building a fresh candidate from C (call it B') and running the same review that produced B.
4. Decide the relationship between C and the candidate: is C an ancestor of B (so B is a fast-forward that already contains C), or did C add work that must be merged/absorbed? Under a strict "reviewed-tip" invariant you re-review C even in the ff case; under a looser "fast-forward-only" invariant a ff push is acceptable. Pick one and encode it — the CAS alone enforces neither review nor ff.
5. Only after C is reviewed and the candidate settled, publish with the tip you just reviewed as the expected old value: `git update-ref refs/heads/release B' C`. If you want to forbid moving the ref backward, also require fast-forward: verify `git merge-base --is-ancestor C B'`, or use `git push --ff-only` instead of a bare CAS.
6. Model this as a bounded loop: read tip -> review -> CAS against that reviewed tip; on CAS failure, go back to read-and-review, never read-and-adopt.

The case the invariant is really meant to catch is when C is *not* an ancestor of B (the other maintainer added new work). There, B discards C's changes, and a blind `update-ref release B C` silently moves the ref over C's commit — the exact overwrite the job must never do.

Source: git-update-ref, https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref — "updates the ... head to <new-oid> only if its current value is <old-oid>"; "If all <ref>s can be locked with matching <old-oid>s ... all modifications are performed. Otherwise, no modifications are performed."

sqlite-connection.question: A support engineer found a REFERENCES clause on song.album_id in our SQLite schema. Does our production writer's current connection enforce foreign keys right now? What can we tell from that schema, and how would we check?
sqlite-connection.answer:
Short answer: unknown — the REFERENCES clause in the schema does not settle it. Whether the writer's connection enforces foreign keys is a per‑connection runtime setting, not something the schema fixes, and we haven't observed the value on that connection.

What the schema does tell you
- `song.album_id` is a child key in a REFERENCES clause pointing at a parent key (the albums table's key). That declares the constraint and its semantics: a referential check on write, plus whatever `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE` action the clause specifies (or NO ACTION if it specifies none).
- It does NOT switch enforcement on. SQLite parses the clause and can list it via `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` even when enforcement is off, so the clause alone can't tell you whether it's actually being enforced.

What still can't be told
- The writer's connection's `PRAGMA foreign_keys` value. Two different values (on vs off) both fit what we know and give opposite answers, so the actual value is unknown until it's read on that connection.

How to check (read‑only, on that target)
- Run `PRAGMA foreign_keys;` on the writer's own connection — the exact connection object doing the writes. It returns one row: `1` = enforcing, `0` = not.
- Per‑connection caveat: the flag is set per connection, so the value you see from another client (e.g. a support engineer opening the same .db file in the `sqlite3` CLI) is that client's value, not the writer's. Don't conflate the two.
- Build caveat: if `PRAGMA foreign_keys;` returns no data instead of `0`/`1`, that SQLite build has FK support compiled out (`SQLITE_OMIT_FOREIGN_KEY` / `SQLITE_OMIT_TRIGGER`) and the pragma is a no‑op — in that case the clause is parsed but never enforced.
- You can also read the writer's connection‑setup code/config to see whether it issues `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` at open time; the authoritative live value is still the pragma read on that same connection.
- Minor: it can't be toggled mid‑transaction (a no‑op outside autocommit), so check it on a clean connection state.

Source: SQLite, "Foreign Key Support" — "Assuming the library is compiled with foreign key constraints enabled, it must still be enabled by the application at runtime, using the PRAGMA foreign_keys command." and "Foreign key constraints are disabled by default (for backwards compatibility), so must be enabled separately for each database connection." https://www.sqlite.org/foreignkeys.html

pg-active-limit.question:
I'm updating an incident note for our west PostgreSQL 16 primary. The support bundle shows one field from pg_settings for max_connections: boot_val = 100. I can't give you a database connection. Can I write that west is currently using 100? What's the smallest check that would settle it?

My notes from the PostgreSQL 16 pg_settings reference: boot_val is what PostgreSQL assumes on startup unless the parameter was set another way. The setting column reports its current value. The same view also has pending_restart for a config change that will need a restart, and sourcefile for the configuration filename where applicable. Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/view-pg-settings.html
pg-active-limit.answer:
No, not from boot_val alone. In the 16 reference, boot_val is "Parameter value assumed at server startup if the parameter is not otherwise set," and `setting` is "Current value of the parameter." boot_val = 100 tells you what west would use at startup if nothing else set the value; it says nothing about whether the running value was set some other way (config file or command line at startup). From that one field, the current value is unknown.

Smallest settling check: the `setting` column for max_connections in the same pg_settings snapshot. If the support bundle's dump captured the full row, it is already in the bundle; pull the whole row rather than just boot_val: setting, source, sourcefile, pending_restart.

Possible results:
- setting = 100: west is currently running with 100, so you can write that. Note the source ('default', a configuration file, or the command line) so the incident note records whether 100 came from the startup default or was explicitly configured.
- setting not 100: the current value is `setting`; don't write 100.
- pending_restart = true: a configuration-file value differs from the running one. Since max_connections is postmaster context, the reference says these settings "can only be applied when the server starts, so any change requires restarting the server" — so the running value is still `setting`, and the config-file value applies only at the next restart.

Fallback if the bundle truly captured only boot_val and no DB access exists: check max_connections in postgresql.auto.conf (highest precedence) and postgresql.conf plus any included .conf files from the bundle. That check gives the configured value, which equals the running value only if it was in place at the last postmaster startup; a config change made after the last restart is not in effect yet. The `setting` column remains the smaller, decisive check.

Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/view-pg-settings.html

pg-source-file.question:
We're checking where the west PostgreSQL 16 primary got max_connections. An on-call account queried pg_settings on that primary and the sourcefile column for max_connections was NULL. The incident note now says “configuration file ruled out.” Is that conclusion warranted, and what read would settle where the value came from? I can't share a database connection here.

My notes from the PostgreSQL 16 pg_settings reference: source identifies the origin of the current parameter value. sourcefile is the configuration filename where the value was set. That field can be null when the value comes from another kind of source. It is also null to a viewer who is neither a superuser nor a member of pg_read_all_settings. The view includes boot_val for the startup assumption and pending_restart for changes waiting on a restart. Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/view-pg-settings.html
pg-source-file.answer:
The conclusion is not warranted. The PostgreSQL 16 `pg_settings` documentation states the `sourcefile` column explicitly:

> Configuration file the current value was set in (null for values set from sources other than configuration files, **or when examined by a user who neither is a superuser nor has privileges of pg_read_all_settings**)

So a NULL `sourcefile` has two distinct causes, and the incident note collapses them into one:

1. The value genuinely did not come from a configuration file.
2. The viewing account lacks the privilege to see the filename, even though the value did come from a configuration file.

An on-call account that is neither a superuser nor a member of `pg_read_all_settings` will see `sourcefile` as NULL for a value set in `postgresql.conf` or `postgresql.auto.conf`. "Configuration file ruled out" is only safe if the querying account had that privilege.

The read that settles it is the `source` column, which is always visible and not gated by privilege:

```sql
SELECT source, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name = 'max_connections';
```

Interpretation of `source`:

- `configuration file` — the value came from a config file; the NULL `sourcefile` was a visibility artifact, and the config file is **not** ruled out.
- `default` — the built-in default (100 in standard builds) is in effect.
- `command line` — set on the server's startup command line (e.g., `postgres -c max_connections=...`).
- `interactive` — set via `SET` in the session that queried it.
- `signal` — changed via SIGHUP.

To also confirm the privilege explanation, the same on-call account can check:

```sql
SELECT rolsuper
FROM pg_roles
WHERE rolname = current_user;

SELECT has_privs_of_role('pg_read_all_settings', current_user);
```

If both return false, the NULL `sourcefile` is fully explained by visibility and says nothing about where the value was set. If either is true, then the NULL does rule out a configuration file, and `source` will point to the actual origin.

Source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/view-pg-settings.html (column `sourcefile`, anchor `id-1.10.5.28.4`)

release-ref.question: Our release job reviewed Git commit A as the current release tip before building candidate B. Another maintainer then moved the release ref to C. The job must never overwrite a tip it hasn't reviewed. Its git update-ref refs/heads/release B A failed. A teammate suggests reading C and automatically retrying the same candidate with C as the expected old value. Should we accept that fallback? What should the job do now?
release-ref.answer:
Short answer: no, not as proposed. Reading C and auto-retrying `update-ref ... B C` would replace an unreviewed tip with a candidate built on A, which is exactly what the old-value guard is there to prevent.

Why the failure is correct, not a glitch

`git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>` is a compare-and-set. Per the reference, with three arguments it "stores the <new-oid> in the <ref> ... after verifying that the current value of the <ref> matches <old-oid>" — it "updates ... to <new-oid> only if its current value is <old-oid>" (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref). So `update-ref refs/heads/release B A` meant "move to B only if the tip is still A." It failed because the tip is now C, not A. That failure is the invariant firing: the job was about to overwrite a tip it had not reviewed, and the CAS stopped it. The old value is a race detector; the whole point is that a conflict means "re-read and re-decide," not "re-assert with the new value."

What the teammate's fallback actually does

Retrying with C as the expected old value changes the assertion to "I'm fine replacing C with B," and then overwrites C with B. But B was built against A, and C was never reviewed. In the general case B and C diverge (B sits on A; C is a sibling the maintainer moved the tip to), so pushing B over C silently discards C's tip position. An existing participant (the other maintainer, or anything tracking the release ref) would next read the release ref and see B where they expect C to still be the tip — C's changes gone from the release line. That's the first observable break of "never overwrite a tip it hasn't reviewed." The word that makes it dangerous is "automatically": a blind re-CAS with a stale candidate, with no re-validation of B against C.

The one case where it's safe

If C is actually an ancestor of B — i.e. B already contains C's content — then C → B is a fast-forward and nothing is lost. Verify that rather than assume it:
  git merge-base --is-ancestor C B && echo "C is in B"
If that holds, then `update-ref refs/heads/release B C` is fine, because the candidate you're installing genuinely incorporates the new tip. (In that scenario you effectively built B after C landed, so confirm that's what happened.)

What the job should do now (concrete)

1. Leave the ref as C. The failed update already did the right thing; don't patch it with a blind `update-ref B` (no old value) — that overwrites whatever the tip is.
2. Re-read the current tip (C).
3. Check the relationship (fast-forward test above).
   - If C is an ancestor of B: safe to CAS `update-ref ... B C`.
   - If not (the usual case): do not push B over C. Rebuild the candidate on top of C — re-run the build/pipeline from C, or rebase B onto C to get B' — review B' against the new tip, then `update-ref ... B' C`.
4. Do this as a CAS retry loop: each iteration re-reads the tip, validates the candidate against that tip, then attempts the CAS. On failure, re-read and repeat. Bound the retries; if the new tip is divergent and carries changes that matter, surface it to a human instead of silently rebasing.

So the teammate's read-C step is correct — it belongs in the loop — but it must be followed by re-validating (and if needed rebuilding) the candidate against C before the next CAS. Accepting "auto-retry B with C" as-is just trades one unreviewed-overwrite for a quieter one.

sqlite-connection.question: A support engineer found a REFERENCES clause on song.album_id in our SQLite schema. Does our production writer's current connection enforce foreign keys right now? What can we tell from that schema, and how would we check?
sqlite-connection.answer:
Short answer to "does it enforce foreign keys right now": the schema alone can't tell you. In SQLite, foreign-key enforcement is a per-connection, runtime switch, not a property of the schema. So the value on your production writer's current connection is unknown unless you read it off that connection. The decisive read is below.

Source: https://www.sqlite.org/foreignkeys.html
- "Assuming the library is compiled with foreign key constraints enabled, it must still be enabled by the application at runtime, using the PRAGMA foreign_keys command."
- "Foreign key constraints are disabled by default (for backwards compatibility), so must be enabled separately for each database connection."
- "The application can also use a PRAGMA foreign_keys statement to determine if foreign keys are currently enabled."
- "It is not possible to enable or disable foreign key constraints in the middle of a multi-statement transaction ... it simply has no effect."

1) What we can and can't tell from that schema
- The schema tells you a foreign key is declared: song.album_id is declared to reference album. In the shorthand form "REFERENCES <parent-table>" the column maps to album's primary key. ("Attaching a 'REFERENCES <parent-table>' clause to a column definition creates a foreign key constraint that maps the column to the primary key of <parent-table>.")
- It does NOT tell you that the constraint is being enforced. Enforcement requires the writer's connection to have PRAGMA foreign_keys ON; the default for a fresh connection is off.
- No ON DELETE / ON UPDATE is specified on that clause, so it defaults to "NO ACTION", and the constraint is immediate by default (violations are caught at the end of the statement; only a DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED declaration defers the check to COMMIT). These details only matter if enforcement is actually on.
- Two caveats worth knowing:
  - The clause being present doesn't even prove the engine can enforce it. If the library was compiled with SQLITE_OMIT_FOREIGN_KEY or SQLITE_OMIT_TRIGGER, foreign keys are parsed but never enforced, and PRAGMA foreign_keys is a no-op.
  - Foreign-key DDL errors are reported at CREATE TABLE time regardless of enforcement, so the fact the table exists validly only means the declaration is syntactically consistent.
- A single successful write that didn't error is just one allowed outcome; it does not prove enforcement is on.

2) How to check it on the production writer
- Read-only, decisive: run  PRAGMA foreign_keys;  on the SAME connection the production writer uses, in autocommit mode. Interpret the result:
    - 1  -> foreign keys ARE enforced on that connection right now.
    - 0  -> declared in the schema but NOT enforced on that connection right now (the default).
    - no row / empty -> this SQLite build doesn't support foreign keys (older than 3.6.19, or compiled with OMIT_FOREIGN_KEY / OMIT_TRIGGER); the PRAGMA is a no-op.
  Why same connection: the setting is per-connection, so opening a fresh connection to check would default to off and mislead you. Why autocommit: toggling it mid-transaction is a no-op, so read the live value outside a transaction.
- Optional behavioral confirmation (reversible): inside a transaction you can roll back, try to INSERT a song row whose album_id has no matching album row. If it fails with "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" (SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_FOREIGNKEY), enforcement is on; if it commits, it's off. Roll back so you don't touch production data.
- Inspect the writer code/driver, which is usually the real source of truth for a connection's value: find where the writer opens its SQLite connection and check whether it issues "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON" after each open (and, if you use a pool, whether it re-issues it per connection). If it never issues it, the value is the driver/library default, which for SQLite is off unless the library or ORM turns it on.

Note: a default value (off) or reproducing the schema on another machine does not establish which value is active on the production writer; only the PRAGMA read on that target does.
